topics.title: Charge and current
topics.summary: Charge comes in whole electrons; current is the number of coulombs passing a point each second, and in a single loop it is the same everywhere.

lensNotes.physics: Charge is conserved, and in a steady DC circuit it can't keep piling up anywhere: a growing excess of charge would set up a field that pushes it back out. So the current into any piece of a circuit equals the current out. The drift speed is v = I/(nAe); copper's n ≈ 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per cubic meter makes it tiny, typically 0.01 to 1 mm/s. A change in the circuit (a switch closing) travels along the wires as an electromagnetic wave at a large fraction of the speed of light, which is why every electron in the loop starts drifting almost at once.
lensNotes.circuit: An ammeter goes in series, so it counts the charge passing that one point; in a single loop it reads the same wherever it is placed. If two meters in what should be one loop disagree, charge is leaving through another path. A battery's mAh rating is a charge: divide it by the load current for an ideal run time, and expect less at high currents or low temperatures.
lensNotes.math: I = Q/t for a steady current. When the current varies, I = dQ/dt, and the charge is the area under the current–time plot, Q = ∫ I dt. Electron counts need powers of ten: dividing by e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is the same as multiplying by 6.24 × 10¹⁸.

formulas.label: Charge of one electron (magnitude; q in the calculator)
Drift speed (n ≈ 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per m³ in copper; A in m²)
Drift time over a length L

goals: Find a current from the charge that passes in a given time (I = Q/t), and turn a battery's mAh rating into coulombs
Convert a current into the number of electrons passing each second
Explain why the current is the same at every point of a single loop, and use that to read ammeters and find faults
Explain why electrons drift at well under a millimeter per second while a lamp lights almost at once
topics.intuition: A metal wire is already full of free electrons, and a current is all of them drifting together, so the same number of coulombs passes every point of a loop each second even though each electron drifts slowly.
topics.why: Matter is made of positive nuclei and negative electrons, and charge is conserved: it is never created or destroyed, only moved. In a metal, about one electron per atom is not bound to any single atom; copper has about 8.5 × 10²⁸ of these free electrons per cubic meter. A battery sets up an electric field along the whole circuit, and that field pushes on every free electron in the loop at once. In the steady state, charge can't keep accumulating anywhere (a growing excess would repel further charge), so whatever charge enters a part each second leaves it each second: the current is the same at every point of the loop. Because the free electrons are so numerous, even an ampere needs only a slow net drift, typically well under a millimeter per second, on top of their fast random motion (around 10⁶ m/s), which averages to zero. The change in the field travels along the wires at a large fraction of the speed of light, so the whole loop starts conducting almost at once. In an insulator the electrons are held in their atoms and bonds, so there are almost no carriers to move.
topics.explanation: Electric charge is measured in coulombs (C). Every electron carries the same tiny charge, −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so one coulomb is about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons. Current is the rate at which charge passes a point: I = Q/t. One ampere is one coulomb per second. Metals conduct because some electrons in each atom are free to move through the whole metal; in an insulator such as PVC or glass they are held by their atoms. A current needs a closed path. In a single loop the same current passes every point: a lamp converts energy, not charge, so the charge leaving it each second equals the charge entering it. Schematics draw conventional current, flowing from + through the circuit to −, the way positive charge would move. In a metal the carriers are electrons, which drift the other way; the current is the same, and formulas and simulators all use the conventional direction. Each electron drifts slowly, well under a millimeter per second, yet a lamp lights at once, because the change in the electric field travels along the wire at a large fraction of the speed of light. A battery's mAh rating is a charge: 1 mAh = 3.6 C.

workedExample.problem: A phone battery is rated 3000 mAh, and the phone draws an average of 250 mA. How much charge can the battery deliver, how long does it last, and how many electrons pass through the battery each second?
steps: Rating as charge: 3000 mAh = 3 A × 1 h = 3 A × 3600 s = 10 800 C (an ampere-second is a coulomb).
Run time: t = Q/I = 10 800 C / 0.25 A = 43 200 s = 12 h. Shortcut: 3000 mAh / 250 mA = 12 h.
Electrons per second: I/e = 0.25 C/s / (1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = 1.56 × 10¹⁸ electrons each second.

The same 0.25 A flows back into the other terminal and through the battery itself (carried by ions inside it): the battery moves charge around the loop and runs down when its chemical reactants are used up, not when it runs out of charge.

Size check: about 12 h is plausible for a phone in moderate use; 12 s or 12 000 h would mean a lost factor of 3600 or 1000. In practice expect somewhat less, because a cell's usable capacity falls at high current and low temperature.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. I (DC), ch. 1 "Basic Concepts of Electricity", section "Conductors, insulators, and electron flow"
sources.note: Free electrons in metals versus bound electrons in insulators such as glass; the effect travels along a conductor almost at once while each electron moves slowly.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. I (DC), ch. 1 "Basic Concepts of Electricity", section "Voltage and current"
sources.note: The rate of charge flow is the same at every point of a simple circuit, and a break anywhere stops the current in the whole loop.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. I (DC), ch. 1 "Basic Concepts of Electricity", section "Conventional versus electron flow"
sources.note: Conventional flow is drawn as positive charge moving from + to −; electrons in a metal move the opposite way.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. I (DC), ch. 2 "Ohm's Law", section "How voltage, current, and resistance relate"
sources.note: One coulomb is about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons, and one ampere is one coulomb passing a point per second.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. II (AC), ch. 14 "Transmission Lines", section "Circuits and the speed of light"
sources.note: The effect of electron motion in a circuit travels at roughly the speed of light while the electrons themselves move nowhere near that fast, so a far-away load responds almost at once.

analogy.text: A bicycle chain is a closed loop of links that all move at once: the same number of links passes every point each second, and no link is used up at the rear sprocket. The pedals deliver energy to the wheel through the chain while the links themselves come back around to the front. Current in a single loop behaves the same way: the same coulombs per second pass every point, and what the load receives is energy, not charge.
analogy.breaksDown: Links push each other by contact, while each electron is pushed by the electric field where it is; a start travels along a chain at about the speed of sound in steel (km/s), but along a circuit at a large fraction of the speed of light. A chain's links all move at one speed, but electrons drift at well under a millimeter per second, faster where the conductor is thinner or has fewer free carriers, and inside the battery ions carry the charge instead. The same current does not mean the same drift speed. A chain has no part where the links give up energy in collisions with a lattice, which is how a resistor turns electrical energy into heat.

templates.prompt: A meter in the wire to a battery's − terminal counts {Q} of charge passing in {t}. Find the average current. (1 mA, one milliamp, is 0.001 A.)
templates.estimateHint: Rounded to one figure: {Q:fig1} C / {t:fig1} s ≈ {IestA} A, which is {Iest}.
templates.explanation: Current is the rate at which charge passes a point. One ampere is one coulomb per second, so coulombs divided by seconds give amperes: I = Q/t = {Q} / {t} = {IA} A. A milliamp (mA) is a thousandth of an ampere (1 mA = 0.001 A), so multiply by 1000: I = {IA} A × 1000 mA/A = {answer}.
hints: Current is the charge passing a point each second.
Divide the charge in coulombs by the time in seconds to get amperes; 1 A = 1000 mA.

misconceptions.feedback: You multiplied. Charge is current × time (Q = I·t), so current is charge ÷ time: I = Q/t.
That's seconds per coulomb, upside down. Current is coulombs per second: I = Q/t.

followUps.prompt: The battery powers a lamp through two wires. A second meter goes in the wire to the battery's + terminal. Over the same {t}, how much charge passes it?

choices.text: The same {Q}: what leaves one terminal comes back into the other
choices.feedback: Right: charge is never used up or created, and it can't keep piling up anywhere in the loop, so as much charge passes the + terminal each second as passes the − terminal.

choices.text: Less than {Q}: the load (whatever the battery powers) used some up
choices.feedback: The load converts energy, not charge. Charge gives up energy as it passes through the load, but none of the charge is lost, so the second meter counts the same {Q}.

choices.text: More than {Q}: the battery's chemicals make extra charge as they react
choices.feedback: The chemicals give the charge energy but create none: charge is conserved. As much charge passes the + terminal as passes the − terminal.

choices.text: None: charge passes only through the battery's − terminal
choices.feedback: Current needs a closed loop. If no charge passed the + terminal, none could keep passing the − terminal either.

followUps.explanation: In a single loop the current is the same at every point, including both battery terminals. Inside the battery the same current is carried by ions (charged atoms and molecules) in the battery's chemicals. What the load takes is energy; the next topic measures the energy each coulomb gives up there as voltage.

templates.prompt: A wire carries a steady {I}. How many electrons pass any point along the wire each second? (Enter a power of ten as 2.5e18 or 2.5 × 10^18.)
templates.explanation: Each electron carries 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and a current of I amps moves I coulombs each second, so the number per second is I/e = {I} / (1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = {answer} electrons per second. One ampere is about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons per second.
hints: One ampere is one coulomb per second. How many electrons make a coulomb?
Divide the current by the electron's charge, e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

misconceptions.feedback: You multiplied by the electron's charge. Each electron carries only 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so it takes a huge number of them to make up the coulombs: divide the current by e.

followUps.prompt: So many electrons pass each second. Does that mean each one moves along the wire quickly?

choices.text: No: copper holds about 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per cubic meter, so this many per second needs only a slow net drift
choices.feedback: Right: the count per second is large because the number of free electrons is enormous, not because any one of them moves fast along the wire.

choices.text: Yes: to get this many through each second they must travel at close to the speed of light
choices.feedback: Only the change in the field travels at a large fraction of the speed of light. The electrons' net drift is slow; there are simply a great many of them crossing the section at once.

choices.text: Yes: electrons have almost no mass, so nothing slows them down
choices.feedback: Something does hold them back: they collide constantly with the vibrating atoms of the metal, which is the wire's resistance and what heats it. But neither mass nor collisions set the drift at a given current: v = I/(nAe), and n is enormous, so the drift is slow. A superconductor (a wire with no resistance at all) carrying the same current drifts just as slowly.

choices.text: No: electrons don't move along a wire at all in DC; only energy moves
choices.feedback: The electrons do drift steadily along a DC circuit; that net drift is the current. It is slow, but it isn't zero.

followUps.explanation: The drift speed is v = I/(nAe). With n ≈ 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ for copper, a few amps in a wire of about 1 mm² gives a drift of a fraction of a millimeter per second. Each electron also moves randomly at around 10⁶ m/s, but that random motion averages to zero and carries no current.

templates.prompt: A battery is rated {cap}h. How much charge can it move through a circuit before it dies? Take the rating at face value.
templates.estimateHint: 1 Ah is 1 A for an hour, and an hour is 3600 s ≈ 4 × 10³ s. So {cap}h is {cap} for an hour: Q ≈ {cap:fig1} A × 4 × 10³ s ≈ {estQ:fig1} C.
templates.explanation: An mAh or Ah rating is a current multiplied by a time, which is a charge. One hour is 3600 s and an ampere-second is a coulomb, so Q = {cap} × 3600 s = {answer}.
hints: A current multiplied by a time is a charge. What is an hour in seconds?
Q = I·t: write the rating as amps times one hour, and the hour as 3600 s.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the rating in ampere-hours. A coulomb is an ampere-second, and an hour is 3600 s, so multiply by 3600.
You converted with 60, which turns hours into minutes. An hour is 3600 seconds, and a coulomb is an ampere-second.

followUps.prompt: Two identical batteries, each rated {cap}h, start fully charged. One runs a load drawing 0.1 A, the other a load drawing 1 A. Taking the rating at face value, how much charge passes through each load before its battery dies?

choices.text: The same charge through each load; the 1 A load just gets through it ten times sooner
choices.feedback: Right: the rating is a fixed charge. The load's current is only the rate at which that charge is drawn, so it sets how long the battery lasts, not how many coulombs pass.

choices.text: Ten times more through the 1 A load, because it draws charge ten times faster
choices.feedback: It draws charge ten times faster, but for a tenth of the time: {tfast} instead of {tslow}. Current × time comes to the same {answer} either way.

choices.text: Ten times more through the 0.1 A load, because it runs ten times longer
choices.feedback: It runs ten times longer, {tslow} instead of {tfast}, but at a tenth of the current. Current × time comes to the same {answer} either way.

choices.text: None through either load: every coulomb that leaves the battery comes back to it
choices.feedback: The charge does come back to the battery, but it passes through the load on the way: a coulomb counter in series with either load would count {answer} in total. Charge returning is why no charge is used up, not why none flows.

followUps.explanation: An mAh or Ah rating is a fixed amount of charge, {answer} here. Current is the rate at which a load draws it, so run time = charge ÷ current: {tslow} at 0.1 A and {tfast} at 1 A. Either way the same coulombs pass through the load. Real cells deliver somewhat less at high currents, which the face-value rating ignores.

templates.noDrawing: about a battery's rating; no circuit to analyze

templates.prompt: Find how long one electron takes, on average, to drift the length shown. This conductor, in a 12 V DC cable feeding an LED light strip, carries a steady current. Copper has about 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per cubic meter. Give the time in hours.
templates.estimateHint: Drift speed first, v = I/(nAe), with every number to one figure and A in m² (1 mm² is 10⁻⁶ m²): A = {Amm} mm², or {Am2:fig1} m² to one figure; n ≈ 9 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ and e ≈ 2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. So v ≈ {I:fig1} A / ({Am2:fig1} m² × 9 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ × 2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) ≈ {vE:fig1} m/s, and t = L/v ≈ {L:fig1} m / ({vE:fig1} m/s) ≈ {tE:fig1} s. An hour is 3600 s ≈ 4 × 10³ s, so t ≈ {tE:fig1} s / (4 × 10³ s/h) ≈ {tH:fig1} h.
templates.explanation: First the drift speed: v = I/(nAe) = {I} / (8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ × {Amm} × 10⁻⁶ m² × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = {v}. Then the time: t = L/v = {L} / {v} = {tsec}, and with 3600 s in an hour that is {answer}. The drift is slow; the current is large only because so many electrons drift together.
hints: Find the drift speed first: the current equals the charge in the free electrons crossing a section per second, I = nAve.
v = I/(nAe), with A in square meters (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m²); then t = L/v, and an hour is 3600 s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the time in seconds, {tsec}. The question asks for hours: an hour is 3600 s, so divide by 3600.
The area must be in square meters: 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m². Leaving it in mm² makes the drift a million times too slow.
You left out the electron's charge. n·A·v counts electrons per second; multiply by e to get coulombs per second, which is the current.
That's the drift speed v = I/(nAe), in meters per second. The question asks for the time to cover {L}: t = L/v.

Two slips here. That's the drift speed v = I/(nAe), not a time, and its area is still in mm², so it comes out a million times too small. Convert the area to m² first (1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m²), which gives v in m/s, then divide the length by it: t = L/v.
Dividing by 60 turns seconds into minutes. An hour is 3600 s, so divide the {tsec} by 3600.
1 mm² = (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m², not 10⁻¹² m² (that is a square micrometer). With the area a million times too small, the drift comes out a million times too fast and the time a million times too short.

You converted the area with 10⁻³, the factor for millimeters. A square millimeter is 10⁻³ m on each side: 1 mm² = 10⁻⁶ m². With the area a thousand times too large, the drift comes out a thousand times too slow and the time a thousand times too long.
That is speed ÷ length, which has units of 1/s, not a time. Time = distance ÷ speed: t = L/v = {tsec}, then divide by 3600 for hours.
That is speed ÷ length, upside down: its units are 1/s, not a time. Time = distance ÷ speed: t = L/v = {tsec}, then divide by 3600 for hours.
Length × speed has units of m²/s, not a time. The time to cover a distance is distance ÷ speed: t = L/v = {tsec}, then divide by 3600 for hours.
Length × speed has units of m²/s, not a time, so dividing it by 3600 gives no hours either. Time = distance ÷ speed: t = L/v = {tsec}, then divide by 3600.
You multiplied by 3600, which turns hours into seconds. {tsec} is already in seconds; an hour is 3600 s, so divide: {tsec} / 3600.

followUps.prompt: The strip has been lit for a minute. At this drift speed, none of the electrons that were at the supply end when the switch closed has reached the strip. Where does the energy the strip turns into light come from?

choices.text: From the supply, through the field: the supply keeps up the field around the loop, and in the strip it pushes the strip's own electrons
choices.feedback: Right: the energy reaches the strip through the electric and magnetic fields along the cable, as fast as a change in the field travels. The electrons in the strip are what the field pushes on there.

choices.text: From electrons arriving from the supply end of the cable, each one bringing along the energy it picked up as it passed through the supply
choices.feedback: None of those electrons has arrived: at this drift speed the trip takes {answer}. The electrons passing through the LEDs now were already in the strip, or next to it, when the switch closed.

choices.text: From the strip's own free electrons, which are used up one by one as the LEDs turn their charge into light and heat
choices.feedback: Charge is conserved: every electron that enters an LED leaves it, and the strip keeps as many free electrons as it started with. The electrons give up energy the field gave them; they are not used up.

choices.text: From the current, which is larger going into the strip than coming out of it, with the difference being turned into light
choices.feedback: The current into the strip equals the current out of it: in a single loop it is the same everywhere. What the strip takes from each coulomb is energy; the next topic measures that energy per coulomb as voltage.

followUps.explanation: Each electron needs {answer} to cross this cable, so the energy can't be riding along with the electrons from the supply. The supply keeps up the field along the loop, and the energy flows from the supply to the strip through the electric and magnetic fields in and around the cable, as fast as a change in the field travels. In the strip, the field pushes the strip's own free electrons through the LEDs. The charge goes around the loop and comes back; the energy is delivered on the way.

templates.prompt: A sensor runs from a battery rated {cap}h and draws a steady {I}. A firmware change cuts its current to {new_I}. What happens to how long the battery lasts? Assume the battery delivers its full rated charge at either current.

feedback.down: The battery holds a fixed charge, and the current is the rate at which the load draws it out: run time = charge ÷ current. Drawing the same charge at a lower rate can't empty the battery sooner.
feedback.same: The rating is a charge (current × time), not a fixed run time. How long that charge lasts depends on how fast the load draws it: run time = charge ÷ current.

templates.explanation: Run time = rated charge / current = {cap}h / {I} = {before}. At {new_I} the same charge lasts twice as long: {after}. Real cells can do a little better than double, because usable capacity rises somewhat at lower current (most for alkaline and lead-acid; barely for lithium-ion, and not at all once the current is well below the rating's test current).
hints: The rating is a fixed amount of charge. How fast is it being drawn?
t = Q/I: halve I and see what happens to t.
templates.noDrawing: about a battery's rating and a load current; no particular circuit

templates.prompt: Replace this wire with a copper one of twice the cross-section (the area of its cut face), carrying the same current. What happens to the electrons' drift speed (their net speed along the wire)?

whatIf.factorIntro: The drift speed is the slow net speed at which the free electrons advance along a wire that carries current. In this wire it is {before} (1 µm/s = 0.001 mm/s), under half a millimeter per second. The free electrons also move at roughly 10⁶ m/s, but in random directions that cancel, so that motion carries no current. A change, such as a switch closing, travels along the wire far faster than the drift: the change in the field moves as an electromagnetic wave, at a large fraction of the speed of light. The current is the charge crossing a section each second, I = nAve (n free electrons per cubic meter, area A, drift speed v, electron charge e), so v = I/(nAe).
whatIf.factorWhy: A is under the line, to the first power, so doubling it halves v.

feedback.down: Twice the cross-section holds twice as many free electrons in each meter of wire. The same coulombs per second are now shared among twice as many carriers, so each one drifts more slowly.
feedback.up: A thicker wire doesn't push its electrons harder. Each meter of it holds more free electrons, so the same coulombs per second are shared among more carriers, and each one needs to drift more slowly.
feedback.same: The current is the same, but each slice of the thicker wire holds more free electrons to share it, so each one carries less of the flow and drifts more slowly.

templates.explanation: The current is the charge crossing a section each second: I = nAve, so v = I/(nAe). With the same current and twice the area, v halves: {before} → {after}. Either way the drift is under half a millimeter per second.
hints: The same current must cross every section. How many free electrons share it in the thicker wire?
v = I/(nAe): the current and n are unchanged, and A doubles.

templates.prompt: A {V} battery drives a current through R1 and a lamp in a single loop. Ammeter A1, in the wire between R1 and the lamp, reads {I}. What does ammeter A2, in the wire between the lamp and the battery's negative terminal, read?

choices.text: {I}, the same as A1
choices.feedback: Right: every coulomb that enters the lamp leaves it. The lamp converts energy, not charge.

choices.text: Less than {I}, because the lamp turns some of the current into light and heat
choices.feedback: The lamp turns energy into light and heat, not charge. Every electron that goes in comes out. The potential energy per coulomb falls across the lamp, which is the voltage across it.

choices.text: Less than {I}, because some electrons stay in the filament to heat it
choices.feedback: Charge can't keep piling up in the filament: a growing excess of electrons would repel the next ones and stop the current. The filament is heated by the electrons' collisions with its atoms, not by keeping electrons.

choices.text: More than {I}, because electrons flow from − to +, so A2 catches them before the lamp uses any
choices.feedback: The direction doesn't change anything: the lamp uses up no charge, so meters on either side of it read the same, whichever way you count the flow.

templates.explanation: Charge is conserved and can't accumulate in a steady circuit, so the same current, {I}, passes every point of the loop: through R1, the lamp, the wires, and the battery. What changes around the loop is the potential energy per coulomb, which the next topic measures as voltage.
hints: Can charge pile up inside the lamp, or disappear in it?
In a single loop there is only one path. What enters each part every second must leave it.

templates.prompt: Schematics mark the direction of a current as conventional current: the way a positive charge would move (a convention fixed before the electron was discovered). In this loop, conventional current flows out of the {V} battery's + terminal, through R1 and the lamp, and back into the − terminal. In the copper wire between the + terminal and R1, which way do the electrons drift?

choices.text: Toward the battery's + terminal, opposite to the conventional current
choices.feedback: Right: conventional current is the direction positive charge would move. Electrons are negative, so they drift the other way, from − around the loop to +.

choices.text: Away from the + terminal, the same way as the conventional current
choices.feedback: Conventional current is defined as the direction positive charge would move. Electrons are negative, so to make the same current they drift the opposite way.

choices.text: Neither: in a metal wire the positive ions carry the current
choices.feedback: The positive ions are fixed in the metal's crystal lattice; they vibrate in place but don't travel. In a metal the carriers are the free electrons.

choices.text: Neither: in DC the electrons only jiggle in place, with no net motion
choices.feedback: Electrons do have fast random motion (around 10⁶ m/s), which averages to zero, but a DC current adds a steady net drift in one direction. That drift is slow, but it is the current.

templates.explanation: Conventional current dates from before the electron was discovered: charge flow was defined as going from + to −. In metals the carriers turned out to be negative electrons, drifting from − through the circuit to +. Positive charge moving one way and negative charge moving the other way are the same current, so the convention never changes a calculated value.
hints: The convention follows a positive charge. What is the sign of an electron's charge?
Electrons are negative. Which way must a negative charge move to make the same current?

followUps.prompt: Schematics, datasheets, and SPICE all use conventional current. Does that give wrong answers in a circuit where the carriers are electrons?

choices.text: No: negative charge moving one way is the same current as positive charge moving the other way
choices.feedback: Right: only the direction of the drawn arrow is a convention. The magnitude, the voltages, and the power are all unchanged.

choices.text: Yes: the voltage signs come out reversed, so engineers flip them at the end of a calculation
choices.feedback: Nothing needs flipping. A current is a rate of charge transfer; −Q moving left transfers charge exactly as +Q moving right does.

choices.text: Yes, but only in semiconductors, where the carriers differ; in plain wires it makes no difference
choices.feedback: In semiconductors both electrons and holes (which act as positive carriers) carry current, and conventional current covers both without any change.

choices.text: No, because in a metal the electrons really do flow from the + terminal to the − terminal
choices.feedback: In a metal, electrons drift from − through the circuit to +. The convention gives right answers because the direction and the sign of the charge flip together, not because electrons go from + to −.

followUps.explanation: Current is the net charge crossing a section per second. Reversing both the sign of the carrier and its direction leaves that number unchanged, so conventional current is a consistent bookkeeping choice, used by every circuit simulator and datasheet.

templates.prompt: A copper wire is covered in PVC insulation. With the circuit running, the copper carries amps along its length, while the current leaking through the PVC is far below a nanoamp. What is the main physical difference between the two materials?

choices.text: Copper has free electrons, about one per atom, that can move through the whole metal; PVC's electrons are all held in atoms and bonds
choices.feedback: Right: a current needs mobile charge carriers. Copper has about 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per cubic meter; PVC has almost none.

choices.text: PVC has no electrons, so there is nothing in it that could carry a current
choices.feedback: PVC is made of atoms like any material and has plenty of electrons. They are bound in its chemical bonds and can't move through the material.

choices.text: Copper's electrons are smaller and lighter, so they slip through the gaps between its atoms
choices.feedback: Every electron is identical: same mass, same charge. What differs is whether an electron is bound to its atom or free to move through the material.

choices.text: PVC absorbs the current flowing into it and turns it into heat inside the insulation
choices.feedback: An insulator doesn't take in and keep charge (if it did, it would become charged). It has almost no free carriers, so hardly any current flows in it at all.

choices.text: A copper atom has more electrons in total than the atoms in PVC, so more of them can flow
choices.feedback: The total number of electrons doesn't matter; most of copper's 29 electrons per atom are tightly bound too. What counts is the outermost one, which in a metal is shared by the whole crystal and free to move.

templates.explanation: Conduction needs mobile charge. In a metal the outermost electron of each atom is shared by the whole crystal, so a field moves these free electrons readily. In an insulator every electron is held in an atom or a bond, and freeing one takes far more energy than room-temperature heat provides, so only a tiny leakage current flows.
hints: What has to be present in a material for charge to flow through it?
Compare how tightly the electrons are held in each material.
templates.noDrawing: about the physics of materials; no circuit to analyze

templates.prompt: An alkaline AA cell dies after 6 hours in a flashlight. What has been used up?

choices.text: Its chemical reactants, because their reaction supplied the lamp's energy
choices.feedback: Right: the cell is a source of energy, not a store of charge; the charge only circulates around the loop. At the − electrode zinc reacts and releases electrons into the wire; at the + electrode manganese dioxide takes electrons back from it. As the zinc and manganese dioxide are used up, the cell's voltage under load sags until it can no longer drive the lamp.

choices.text: Its electrons, because it pushed its store of them out into the circuit
choices.feedback: Every electron that leaves the − terminal is matched by one arriving at the + terminal, so the cell never runs short of charge. A cell that had pushed out a store of electrons would be strongly charged, and it isn't.

choices.text: The current, because the lamp used some of it up on each pass
choices.feedback: The current is the same everywhere in the loop, on both sides of the lamp. The lamp converts energy, not charge.

choices.text: The wire's free electrons, because they all passed through the lamp
choices.feedback: The wire's free electrons are never used up; they drift around the loop and stay in the circuit. The energy the lamp turns into light and heat comes from the cell's chemistry, through the field in the circuit.

templates.explanation: Charge is conserved, so the cell can't run out of it. Its chemical reaction does work on the charge passing through it, and the energy each coulomb gives up in the lamp becomes light and heat. As the zinc and manganese dioxide react, the cell's voltage under load sags; at a flashlight's current it dies while some of them are still unreacted. Its mAh rating counts how much charge it can drive around the circuit before that, at a stated current: drawn harder, it delivers less.
hints: Does any charge leave the circuit while the flashlight is on?
Compare the charge leaving the − terminal with the charge arriving at the + terminal.
templates.noDrawing: about what a battery does, not a particular circuit

templates.prompt: Ammeters A1 and A2 are in the loop: the current passes through each. Find the fault that explains the readings.

faults.text: The lamp's filament has burned through, leaving a gap inside the lamp
faults.feedback: A burned-through filament leaves a gap in the only path, so no current would flow anywhere: both meters would read 0 A.
faults.why: Both meters read 0 A: the burned-through filament leaves a gap in the only path, and a break anywhere in a single loop stops the current everywhere in it.

faults.text: An extra resistor (a part that conducts, like R1) joins the wire between R1 and A2 to the battery's − terminal
faults.feedback: That resistor would give charge a second way back to the − terminal, leaving the loop between the meters: A1 would read more than A2, and the difference would flow through the extra resistor.
faults.why: A1 reads more than A2, which a single loop never allows: charge is leaving the loop between the meters. The extra resistor gives it a second way back to the − terminal, and the difference, A1 − A2, flows through it. A1 changes too, because the extra path changes how much current the battery drives; how much is Ohm's law, two topics on.

faults.text: An extra resistor joins the battery's + terminal, before A1, to the wire between R1 and A2
faults.feedback: That resistor would carry charge from the + terminal around A1 and R1, joining the loop between the meters: A2 would read more than A1, and the difference would flow through the extra resistor.
faults.why: A2 reads more than A1: charge is joining the loop between the meters. The extra resistor carries it from the + terminal around A1 and R1, and the difference, A2 − A1, flows through it. A1 changes too, because the extra path changes how much current the battery drives; how much is Ohm's law, two topics on.

templates.explanation: In a single loop, two ammeters must agree: charge can't pile up or vanish between them. Both at zero: a break somewhere in the loop. A1 above A2: charge leaves the loop between the meters, through a second path. A2 above A1: charge joins the loop between the meters, from a second path.
hints: First compare A1 with A2. When can two meters in one loop disagree?
Current flows from the + terminal through A1, R1 and then A2. Charge that leaves the loop between the meters never reaches A2; charge that joins between them passes A2 but not A1.

explanationSteps.text: In a single loop, two ammeters must agree: charge can't pile up or vanish between them.
Both at zero: a break somewhere in the loop.
A1 above A2: charge leaves the loop between the meters, through a second path.
A2 above A1: charge joins the loop between the meters, from a second path.

templates.prompt: Find the electrons' drift speed in this conductor (the net speed at which its free electrons advance along it), in meters per second. The current is steady. Copper has about 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per cubic meter. Enter the number only, with a power of ten as 3e-9 or 3 × 10^-9.
templates.explanation: In one second, the free electrons in a length v of the conductor cross a section, so the current is the charge they carry: I = nAve, and v = I/(nAe). With the area in square meters, {Amm} mm² = {Amm} × 10⁻⁶ m²: v = {I} / (8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ × {Amm} × 10⁻⁶ m² × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = {v} (1 µm/s = 10⁻⁶ m/s). The free electrons in each meter of this conductor carry {Qm} in all, which is why so slow a drift carries amps.

templates.prompt: Estimate the electrons' drift speed in this conductor without a calculator: which is closest? Copper has about 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per cubic meter.

choices.text: About 10⁻⁴ m/s: a tenth of a millimeter each second
choices.feedback: Right: the free electrons in each meter of this conductor carry {Qm} in all, so passing {I} needs them to advance only {v}.

choices.text: About 1 m/s: one meter of conductor each second
choices.feedback: A drift that fast would carry over a thousand times this current. The free electrons in each meter of this conductor carry {Qm} in all, so passing {I} needs them to advance only {v}.

choices.text: About 10³ m/s: a kilometer of conductor each second
choices.feedback: Free electrons do move that fast and faster, around 10⁶ m/s, but in random directions: that motion averages to zero and carries no current. The net drift the field adds is only {v}, because each meter of conductor holds {Qm} of free-electron charge.

choices.text: About 2 × 10⁸ m/s: two-thirds of the speed of light
choices.feedback: That is roughly how fast a change in the field travels along a cable, not how fast the electrons move. A drift that fast would carry over a billion times this current; with {Qm} of free-electron charge in each meter, {I} needs only {v}.

templates.explanation: The current is the charge in the free electrons crossing a section each second: I = nAve, so v = I/(nAe) = {I} / (8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ × {Amm} × 10⁻⁶ m² × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) = {v}: of the four options, nearest to 10⁻⁴ m/s, a tenth of a millimeter each second. To one figure: n·e ≈ 9 × 10²⁸ × 2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C ≈ 2 × 10¹⁰ C per cubic meter, so each meter of a 1 mm² conductor (10⁻⁶ m²) holds about 2 × 10⁴ C of free-electron charge, and an ampere moves it about 1/(2 × 10⁴) m = 5 × 10⁻⁵ m each second. The drift is slow because the free electrons are so many.

templates.prompt: Each free electron takes about {thours} to drift the length of this cable, yet current starts flowing in the 12 V light strip at the cable's far end within a fraction of a microsecond of closing a switch at the supply end. Why?

choices.text: Free electrons already fill the loop, and the change in the field travels along the cable at a large fraction of the speed of light
choices.feedback: Right: the carriers at the far end were already there. What travels fast is the change in the electric field, not the electrons.

choices.text: Electrons near the switch rush to the strip in the first instant after it closes; the slow drift only sets in once the current is steady
choices.feedback: Even at switch-on the drift stays a small fraction of a millimeter per second: hours to cross the cable. The carriers in the strip don't need to come from the switch; they are already there.

choices.text: Electrons leave the switch at nearly the speed of light, then slow down to the drift speed once the strip draws its full current
choices.feedback: No electron makes that trip quickly. It is the field, set up along the wires as an electromagnetic wave, that arrives at a large fraction of the speed of light, and it moves the carriers already at the far end.

choices.text: The light strip holds a store of charge that keeps it lit until the electrons from the switch arrive at the far end, hours later
choices.feedback: A light strip doesn't run on stored charge, and electrons from the switch would take hours to arrive. The carriers already in the strip and the cable start moving as soon as the field reaches them.

templates.explanation: Two speeds are at work. The electrons drift at {v}, so each takes about {thours} to cover {L}. The change in the field travels along the cable as an electromagnetic wave at a large fraction of the speed of light (about two-thirds of it in a plastic-insulated cable, so {L} takes about {tprop}). The cable and the strip are full of free electrons from the start, so current flows in the strip as soon as the field reaches it, and it lights essentially at once.
hints: Where are the free electrons that flow through the strip just after the switch closes?
Two things move: the electrons, and the change in the field that pushes them. Which one has to reach the strip?

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. II (AC), ch. 14 "Transmission Lines", section "Circuits and the speed of light"
sources.note: The effect of electron motion in a circuit travels at roughly the speed of light while the electrons themselves move nowhere near that fast, so a far-away load responds almost at once.
